chapter_theme: Gift poems to the hill chieftains Pekan, Nalli, Ori, the lord of Konkanam, Erai and Kumanan: the guide poems, the cycle pleading with Pekan to return to his wife, the roll of seven dead givers, and the bard's starving household pressed on Kumanan.

141.reading: A bard resting on the road with his chariot unyoked, wearing a gold lotus and with his viṟali garlanded, answers a hungry bard who keeps asking who they are: before they saw Pekan they were poorer than he is, for Pekan, who gave a cloak to a peacock knowing it could neither wear nor wrap it, gives not with an eye to the next world but with an eye to other people's want.
141.nuance: The cloak given to a peacock is offered as proof of motive: a gift to a creature that can neither use it nor repay it cannot be a bid for merit, so Pekan's famous folly becomes the evidence that he looks only at others' need (வறுமை நோக்கின்று), not at the next world (மறுமை). The guide also admits that he was once poorer than the man he guides (நின்னினும் புல்லியேம்).

thinai_evidence.note: a guide's praise of a patron's giving, which is paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the rewarded bards resting at ease in the wild tract

142.reading: Like the rain that by its unbounded habit pours into the drained tank, over the broad field, and wastes itself on salt land where it helps no one, Pekan of the rutting elephant and warrior's anklet is foolish only in giving, never foolish in battle when other armies come at him.
142.nuance: கொடைமடம், folly in giving, is a fault named as praise: the poet concedes that Pekan gives without discrimination, as rain falls on salt land, then pairs it with the folly he lacks (படைமடம்), so the one fault becomes the measure of his greatness in the other field.

thinai_evidence.note: plain praise of a patron's giving and valour

comparisons.tenor: Pekan's giving, which falls on the deserving and undeserving alike

143.reading: Kapilar addresses Pekan, lord of a hill where the Kuravar, having made offerings to the god about the rain and rejoicing that it turned as they asked, eat their millet, and asks who that pitiable woman was who yesterday, in a small village by the waterfalls, when his hungry troupe stood at her door praising Pekan and his hill, could not stop her tears and wept aloud, wetting her breast, like a lamenting flute.
143.nuance: The poet never says the woman is Pekan's wife: the question யார்கொல் அளியள் leaves him to supply the answer, and it is the song in his praise that makes her weep, so the praise poem turns into the reproach. The hill people whose prayer was answered stand at the opening against a woman whose waiting is not.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman's weeping for an absent husband told to the man himself, which is the unmatched love of perunthinai

comparisons.tenor: the woman's sobbing

144.reading: Paranar tells Pekan that his want of pity is cruel: when the bards at nightfall played the sevvazhi mode and sang of his forest that meets the rains, a woman whose kohl-lined eyes outshone the neythal flower wept until her tears wet her ornaments, and when they bowed and asked whether she was kin to their patron she wiped her eyes with fingers like kaanthal buds and said she was not, only that he is said to drive there always in his loud chariot, desiring the beauty of a woman like her, to the good town fenced with mullai.
144.nuance: Asked whether she is his kin, she denies being his kin and names the other woman only as one 'like me', so the wife's restraint carries the rebuke the poet does not make himself. The cycle 143 to 147 shows several poets taking up one patron's domestic breach in turn.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife weeping for a husband who goes to another woman, told to him by the bards

comparisons.tenor: her kohl-lined eyes, more beautiful than the flower
her fingers

145.reading: Paranar reminds Pekan, famed for giving a cloak to the peacock in pity lest it shiver, that the bards come neither from hunger nor with a burden to lay down: the gift they beg, playing the small lute until listeners tremble and crying 'do this dharma, lover of grace', is that he mount his chariot tonight and end the grief of the woman who lives in sorrow.
145.nuance: The peacock is turned against Pekan: if he pitied a bird that might be cold, he cannot leave a woman in sorrow. By declaring that they are not hungry, the bards empty the parisil form of its usual content and make it a plea for reconciliation.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife abiding in grief for an absent husband, which the bards plead for

comparisons.tenor: the dark stem of the small lute

146.reading: Arisil Kizhar tells Pekan to keep his rare jewels and wealth: if, after the bard has sung his good hard-soiled land in the sevvazhi mode, he wishes to give a gift, let it be that his wife, who wastes away in grief at his neglect, may perfume her soft hair, thick as a peacock's gathered tail, with fragrant smoke and wear a cool garland, and that his horses be yoked to his tall chariot.
146.nuance: The gift is described entirely through the wife's toilet: the incense and the garland she has given up will come back when he does, so the poem asks for his return without stating it, and ends by commanding his horses rather than him.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife enduring her husband's neglect, the gift asked being his return

comparisons.tenor: her thick soft hair

147.reading: Perunkunrur Kizhar tells the lord of the Aviyar that he has crossed many hills of cave-fed falls playing the sevvazhi mode, and that the gift he asks is this: that the lovely woman with streaked, rain-dark eyes, who heard alone yesterday the sweet rumble of the dark clouds and lives in one corner in loneliness, should wash clean as an earth-dulled gem her dark hair left without oil and crowd it with fresh flowers, if he goes back today.
147.nuance: The rain-cloud heard 'yesterday' is the season of promised return, so the gift is set against a deadline already passed; hair left without oil (நெய்யொடு துறந்த) is the sign of a wife who has given up adornment while she waits, and the poet asks for it to be reversed today.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife living alone through the rains her husband was to return by

comparisons.tenor: her hair washed clean of its neglect

148.reading: Nalli of the high hill loud with falls: having praised his tireless strength and the wealth people long for, the poet has been given daily, in his bright great house, fine jewels with elephants, gifts in full, so that his small red tongue no longer knows how to recite deeds never done in seeking praise from kings without merit.
148.nuance: The poem praises by renouncing a genre: Nalli's gifts have made flattery unnecessary, so the poet's honesty is counted among the things Nalli gave him. It also admits that bards did invent deeds for meaner patrons.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron's giving through its effect on the poet's speech

149.reading: Long live Nalli: because of the generosity with which he has taken on the duty of keeping them, the poet's people have forgotten the order of their modes, playing marutham in the hushed evening and sevvazhi in the morning.
149.nuance: The praise is a joke against the bards: plenty has done what hunger never did and made them lose the clock of their own craft, since each mode had its hour. The poem asks for nothing, which is why the colophon's பரிசில் sits awkwardly on it.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron through what his giving has done to the bards

150.reading: In a cloak torn like an autumn kite's dark wing, the poet lay at the foot of a jack tree, past caring for himself, when a strong-bowed hunter with a gem on his head and an anklet bloody from killing deer saw his weariness, made him sit as he rose to bow, roasted white fat on a fire he struck himself before his men caught up, and bade him eat with his kin; when the poet had eaten, drunk at the cool falls and made to leave, the hunter said a forest people have no other rare treasure and gave him the chain from his chest and the bracelet from his arm, told neither his country nor his name, and only from others did the poet learn that he was Nalli, lord of the hill guarded by Thotti.
150.nuance: The poem turns on what Nalli withholds, his country and his name, so the gift comes without the fame it usually buys, and the poet repays him by naming him in the last line. He cooks with his own fire before his attendants arrive. Line 25 plays on தோட்டி, an elephant goad and the name of the hill: a goad 'not forged of iron'.

thinai_evidence.note: a patron's giving told as an encounter, plain praise

comparisons.tenor: the poet's tattered cloak
the white fat of the kill
the sweet water of the hill

151.reading: The poet tells the young Vicchi lord why he embraced Kandeerakkon and not him: Kandeerakkon is of a house so generous that when the lord of the sky-touching hill is away even its women give jewelled young she-elephants to delight singers as of old; the Vicchi lord, kin of Nannan of the golden chariot, would also have deserved an embrace, but because of a door shut against singers the poet's people have shunned his fragrant great hill where the clouds pour.
151.nuance: An embrace was a public honour that a poet could give or withhold, and this poem justifies a public snub. Whose door was shut, the young lord's or his line's, is not certain from the text. The irrealis மன்னே ('you would have been fit') keeps the refusal courteous.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of one patron set against blame of another

152.reading: The poet tells how he met a hunter whose one arrow felled an elephant, passed through a gape-mouthed tiger, rolled a spotted stag, dropped a boar and lodged in an iguana in an anthill; guessing that this rich killer, plainly no man who sells, might be Ori, lord of the fruitful hill, he had his viṟali and troupe set up drum, lute, horn and pipes and played all twenty-one modes in order, and when they hailed him as 'king' the man was abashed because it was his own name and, not letting them go, gave them the meat of his kill, toddy like melted ghee and gold and gems from his hill, there in the wilderness: the lord of tall Kolli, eager for unguarded giving.
152.nuance: The single arrow through five beasts is the poem's credential for the man before he is named, and the bards test their guess by performance: hailed as கோ, he is abashed because it is his own name. As in 150, the patron is met as a hunter in the forest, not at court.

thinai_evidence.note: the patron's giving and the bard's dismissal with gifts

comparisons.tenor: the hunter, who does not look like one who sells his kill
the toddy

153.reading: The poet's troupe of performers went to see the rain-like giving of Athan Ori, lord of the cloud-clad hill who daily gives jewelled elephants to suppliants, and received garlands of gold lilies on white fibre that no cold water ever bloomed, ornaments and herds of elephants; now, perhaps because they are no longer hungry, they will neither dance nor sing to their tight-strung drums.
153.nuance: The lilies 'that do not bloom in cold water' are gold work, so even the flowers are imperishable; and the closing joke, that the troupe stopped performing when it stopped being hungry, admits that the bards' art ran on need.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron through the wealth of his bards

comparisons.tenor: Ori's giving

154.reading: Even beside the wave-beaten sea people ask someone they know for a little water to quench their thirst, and so poets, though they live among kings, go to the faultlessly generous; the poet therefore does not ask what he will get, but came because he thought of the patron: to say 'give' is hard, but whether he gives or not, singing his valour that does not run from thrown spears and his great forest of Konkanam, where cool falls come down like spread white cloth, is easy.
154.nuance: Kings are the sea, vast and undrinkable; the generous small lord is the little sweet water got from someone known. The poet separates what parisil poems usually join: asking is hard for him, praising is easy, so the praise is offered as free.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet's approach to a patron for a gift, parisil under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: poets who live among kings but go to the generous
the falls of the patron's forest

155.reading: Bard who hug the small curved-stemmed lute to your wasted side and cry out for someone to understand and end your distress, listen: as the pale white flower of the nerunchi in a deserted village opens to face the rising sun, the bowls of needy poets open in bloom when they face the cool-garlanded chest of the lord of Konperunkanam of shining fame.
155.nuance: The image is a weed of the deserted village that turns to the sun, so the poor are flowers of a ruined place and the patron is their sun; the flower's colour is பசலை, the word akam keeps for the pallor of lovesickness.

thinai_evidence.note: one bard directing another to a patron, aatruppadai under paadaan

comparisons.vehicle: நெருஞ்சிப் பசலை வான்பூ ஏர்தரு சுடரின் எதிர்கொண்டு
comparisons.tenor: the poor poets' bowls opening toward the patron

156.reading: Other hills have one good thing, but Konperunkanam always has two: it will lie open for the suppliants who come to it in desire to gather and eat, and besides that it has the lord who sends kings with numberless armies home after taking their tribute.
156.nuance: The poem counts a hill's goods like assets: the land itself feeds suppliants, and the lord feeds it with kings' tribute, so giving and conquest are two products of one place.

thinai_evidence.note: plain praise of a patron's land and conquest

157.reading: Bearing with the faults of one's own kin, feeling shame at others' destitution, having a strength that never brings disgrace on the army, and walking tall in the assembly of kings are not fitting for your lords; they fit our Erai, chief of the Kuravar, with broad chest, killing spear and kodal chaplet, lord of the great hill on whose cloud-cleared heights, at dusk, a fine stag that has lost its herd and cannot find its lair calls to its young doe while the spotted tiger in the rock cave listens.
157.nuance: The virtues are those the Kural later files under shame and forbearance, claimed here by a woman poet of the Kuravar for her own hill chief against other men's lords. Who நும்மோர் ('your people') are is not certain. The closing scene of the stag, the doe and the listening tiger is left without comment.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a hill chief's virtues

158.reading: Now that the seven are dead who fought and gave, Pari of Parambu, Ori who ruled Kolli, Malaiyan who rode Kari to victory, Ezhini of the horse held but not ridden, Pekan of the great hill guarded by a god, Ay whom Mosi sang, and Nalli who drove off his foes and gave without refusing, the poet has hurried here thinking of Kumanan to end the need of suppliants, and blesses the lord of Muthiram, where a male monkey that has eaten an old thorny jackfruit calls his soft-headed mate with his hand, that his spear may prevail over his enemies along with his famed generosity.
158.nuance: The roll of seven makes generosity a line of succession with a gap that Kumanan is invited to fill, so the praise is also a summons. Each giver gets one emblem, compressing whole poems into an epithet. 'The horse held but not ridden' (ஊராது ஏந்திய குதிரை) may be Ezhini's hill named Kuthirai; the text does not settle it.

thinai_evidence.note: a blessing on a patron, with a plea for gifts

159.reading: The poet's mother, so old she complains that her life will not leave her, walks in short steps on a stick, hair like spread thread, never past the yard; his wife, pale and worn, her breasts dried by the many small children who knead and suck them, boils without salt the unripe shoots of rubbish-heap greens, forgets rice, eats the greens without buttermilk and, in soiled scant cloth, goes without and does not blame virtue; so that both their hearts and his hungry kin may rejoice, as cloud pours on a hunters' burnt clearing whose millet would not ear, he will not take a gift given grudgingly though it were a tusked killer elephant, but given gladly he will take even a kunri seed's worth, and asks Kumanan to grant it so.
159.nuance: After the longest picture of household hunger in the chapter, the demand is about manner, not size: an elephant given grudgingly is refused and a kunri seed given gladly accepted, so the bard puts the giver's gladness above his family's need. அறம் பழியா, his wife does not blame virtue though she starves, gives the household its own pride.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard pressing a patron for a gift, parisil kadaanilai

comparisons.tenor: the old mother's white hair
the patron's gift reviving the starving household

160.reading: Told by Kumanan's praisers that this lord of Muthiram, who flings away hard-won gold vessels so that the bards' troupe may not fail, would revive him like rain on a sun-scorched forest with rich seasoned rice and ghee served in small gold dishes ringed like stars around the moon, the poet hurried, driven by his heart, from a house where his little tufted son sucks his mother's milkless breast and cries opening the empty pots, while she quiets him with the tiger and the moon and at last asks him to show how he sulks when he thinks of his father; and he asks to be sent off quickly with lasting wealth so that she who suffers in waking life may flourish, and will praise Kumanan's fame across the sea-girt earth.
160.nuance: Lines 1 to 14 quote the hearsay that brought him, so the poem holds Kumanan to a reputation. The mother uses the tiger and the moon, the props of nursery talk, in place of food. Four lines are flagged as possible misprints and the review finds two lines missing, so details of the household scene are not secure.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard pressing a patron for a quick gift

comparisons.vehicle: முளிபுல் கானம் குழைப்பக், கல்லென அதிர்குரல் ஏறோடு துளிசொரிந் தாங்கு
comparisons.tenor: Kumanan's food reviving a starving body
the small gold dishes ringed around the rice

links.note: 141 says Pekan's giving does not look to the next world (மறுமை நோக்கின்றோ அன்றே) but to others' want; Kural 222 says giving alone is good even if there were no higher world.
links.teaches: The Kural's hypothetical, giving is good even without heaven, is already the bards' test of a true patron, and 141 adds the positive motive the couplet leaves unstated: the giver looks at the receiver's want, as the useless gift to the peacock proves.

links.note: 141 cites the cloak given to the peacock as proof that Pekan gives without calculation; 145 cites the same cloak (படாஅம் ஈத்த) to plead for his abandoned wife.
links.teaches: The peacock story served the bards both ways: as praise of pure giving in 141 and as leverage in 145, where a patron famous for pitying a bird is shamed into pitying his wife, so a patron's legend could be used against him.

links.note: Both liken giving to rain; Kural 211 makes the rain a duty that asks no return, while 142 notes that rain also wastes itself on salt land and calls Pekan's giving கொடைமடம், folly.
links.teaches: The Kural keeps only the dutiful side of the rain image, but the Purananuru poet saw its waste as well, so the rain figure for generosity carried an admitted cost of indiscrimination that the maxim leaves out.

links.note: 143 asks who the weeping woman at the door was (யார்கொல் அளியள்) without answering; 144 tells the same kind of scene and lets the woman answer that she is no kin of Pekan's and that he goes to another woman.
links.teaches: Read in sequence, the Pekan poems work as a cycle in which each poet adds what the last withheld: Kapilar leaves the woman unnamed, Paranar gives her a voice and names the cause, so the reproach of a patron was built up by several poets in turn.

links.note: Paranar rebukes Pekan in 144 for leaving his wife for another woman; Paranar in Akananuru 262 has a lover compare his beloved's fragrance to Pekan's rain-cloud hill (வண்மகிழ்ப் பேகன் கொண்டல் மாமலை).
links.teaches: The same poet uses Pekan's hill as a sweet image of union in akam while rebuking Pekan's own broken marriage in puram, so the patron's name entered akam similes as pure fame, cleansed of the scandal the puram poems record.

links.note: In 150 a strong-bowed hunter feeds the poet, gives his chain and will not tell his name, and is Nalli; in 152 a hunter who killed five beasts with one arrow is abashed when hailed as king, gives the meat of his kill, and is Ori.
links.teaches: Two poets tell the same scene of a chieftain met as an unnamed hunter in the forest who feeds the bard from his kill, so the incognito hunter-giver was a recognised type of patron story, in which the gift is proved genuine by being given before the giver is known.

links.note: Akananuru 238 names Nalli for rain-like giving of chariots and elephants to suppliants (மழைசுரந் தன்ன ஈகை) as a simile's backdrop; 150 tells one of his gifts in full, a chain from his chest given to a ragged poet in the forest.
links.teaches: The akam epithet compresses into a formula of chariots and elephants a fame that the puram poem shows was made of personal, unannounced gifts, so the akam poet's shorthand assumes hearers who knew stories like 150.

links.note: 151 praises the house of Kandeerakkon, where women give she-elephants when the lord is away; 150 shows Nalli, whom the colophons call Kandeerakkon, giving while concealing his name.
links.teaches: Both poems praise this house for giving that does not wait on the lord being seen as giver, by his women in his absence or by himself unnamed, so the Kandeera fame was for giving as a household habit, not a court performance.

links.note: 151 explains a snub: the poets shunned the hill of Nannan's kin because of a door shut against singers; Akananuru 152 praises Nannan for famous giving, flinging elephants (இசைநல் ஈகைக் களிறுவீசு). On the reading that the same line of Nannan is meant, the two reputations are incompatible.
links.teaches: Whether one Nannan or two, the name carried opposite reputations for giving in the two anthologies, which shows that a patron's fame among bards was contested and could be undone by one shut door.

links.note: 149 says Nalli's giving made the bards forget the hours of their modes; 153 says Ori's gifts made the troupe stop dancing and singing, since they were no longer hungry.
links.teaches: Two poets praise two patrons with the same joke, that plenty spoils the performer's craft, which shows that the bards themselves saw their art as driven by need and counted its loss as the fullest proof of a gift.

links.note: 154 makes asking for a little water from someone known the natural image for seeking out the generous; Kural 1066 says even asking water for a cow is the greatest degradation of the tongue. On the plain reading the same act is natural in one and shameful in the other.
links.teaches: The bard and the moralist used the same smallest request in opposite ways: for the poet it shows that seeking the generous is as natural as thirst, for the Kural it shows that no request is small enough to be clean, though 154 itself concedes that asking is hard (இரத்தலோ அரிதே).

links.note: 154 says the thirsty by the sea ask a known person for a little water; 204 says the thirsty do not drink from the great sea but find many paths to drinking water, even if muddied by cattle.
links.teaches: The sea that cannot quench thirst was a shared figure for great but useless wealth, and the two poets turn it differently: 154 uses it to explain why poets pass by kings, 204 to say a refused seeker should go elsewhere without blaming the giver.

links.note: 157 counts among Erai's virtues being ashamed at others' destitution (பிறர் கையறவு தான் நாணுதல்); Kural 1015 calls those who feel shame for others' disgrace as for their own the dwelling of shame.
links.teaches: The Kural's widened shame, felt for what others suffer, appears first as a chief's virtue praised by a woman poet of his hill, where its object is concretely other people's want rather than their disgrace in general.

links.note: 158 lists Malaiyan (who rode Kari) and Ori among the seven dead givers; Akananuru 209 says Kari of Mullur killed Ori and gave Kolli to the Cheras (ஓரிக் கொன்று சேரலர்க்கு ஈத்த).
links.teaches: The canon of the seven givers sets side by side two men one of whom killed the other, so the list honours giving alone and is silent about the wars among the givers, which the akam poet remembers in a simile.

links.note: 158 names 'Ori of the strong bow who ruled Kolli' (கொல்லி ஆண்ட வல்வில் ஓரி) in one line; 152 tells the hunt in which his single arrow passed through five beasts and the gifts he gave the bards.
links.teaches: The epithet in the roll-call condenses an exploit that 152 tells whole, so the list of seven assumed an audience that knew the separate poems on each giver.

links.note: 159 will refuse an elephant given grudgingly and take a kunri seed given gladly; Kural 1057 says the heart rejoices on seeing those who give without scorn.
links.teaches: The Kural names the asker's joy at a gift without contempt; 159 turns it into a rule of conduct for the asker, who must refuse a grudging gift even while his family starves, so the manner of giving decided whether a bard could accept at all.

links.note: Kural 1061 says not asking even from those who give gladly is worth ten million times more; 159 treats asking a glad giver as honourable and refuses only the grudging gift.
links.teaches: The bard's code and the Kural's draw the line of dignity in different places: for the bard the giver's gladness makes asking clean, for the Kural even the gladdest giver does not, so the Kural's chapter on the dread of asking rejects the very compromise the parisil poems lived by.

links.note: 160 and 164, by different poets to the same Kumanan, both show the poet's child sucking his mother's milkless breast and crying (வறுமுலை), with empty cooking pots.
links.teaches: Two poets bring Kumanan the same picture of the child at the dry breast, so the starving household was a set piece of the parisil kadaanilai addressed to this patron, not one poet's private confession.

links.note: 160 asks to be sent off quickly (வல்லே விடுதல் வேண்டுவல்); Naladiyar 111 says keeping a seeker waiting till hope dies is worse than ingratitude.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar faults delay as the giver's breach of truth; 160 shows what the delay costs at the other end, a mother distracting a hungry child at home, which is why the bard asks for speed before size.

new_concepts.gloss: the gift a bard seeks from a patron, and the asking for it
new_concepts.label_source: the verses use the word: பரிசில் in 145 line 8, 146 line 5, 147 line 9, 148 line 4, 151 line 4 and 159 line 23; the colophons of 148, 149, 152, 154, 158 to 160 use it in their thurai

new_concepts.gloss: a guide poem in which one performer directs another to a patron
new_concepts.label_source: the colophon thurai names it: பாணாற்று படை and புலவராற்றுப் படை (141), பாணாற்றுப்படை (155)

source_issues: 141: the colophon thurai reads பாணாற்று படை, without the doubled ப் of பாணாற்றுப்படை (as in 155); name normalised in puram_thurai.

142: the review's line table says sangamtamil.com lacks our line 1; our line 1 (அறுகுளத்து உகுத்தும், அகல்வயல் பொழிந்தும்) is the first of the three places the rain falls and the simile needs it, so it is marked as part of the poem.

143 to 147: these are puram poems on akam matter (a patron's neglected wife), marked akam_puram mixed with thinai perunthinai, as their colophons have it; the bard who pleads is coded as paanan speaking to the thalaivan.
147: line 5 is flagged as repeated in 349 line 5 (a formula for a woman's eyes); line 6 has an edition variant noted in the flags, our reading kept.
148 line 3: கனிற்றொடு looks like a misprint for களிற்றொடு (with elephants); marked as elephant.
149: the colophon thurai is பரிசில், but the poem asks for nothing and states the effect of Nalli's giving, which fits இயன்மொழி (the review notes the site's Iyan Mozhi); colophon kept as is.
